nameStory: The Sigmoid Prominent gets its name from the distinctive curved, S-shaped marking on its forewings that resembles the mathematical symbol called a sigmoid. The word 'prominent' refers to the family's characteristic of having tufts of scales that stick up from their wings and body when at rest, giving them a distinctive bumpy profile.
description: The Sigmoid Prominent is a medium-sized moth with a wingspan of about 1 to 1.5 inches across. It belongs to the prominent moth family, known for their fuzzy, somewhat chunky appearance and habit of resting with their wings held tent-like over their bodies. These nocturnal moths are most active during the warmer months and are drawn to lights at night. Their caterpillars feed exclusively on poplar and willow trees.

idTips.label: Sigmoid wing marking
idTips.description: Look for the distinctive S-shaped or curved line marking on the forewings that gives this moth its name - it appears as a pale, whitish sigmoid curve against the darker wing background

idTips.label: Wing size and span
idTips.description: Medium-sized with wings spanning 28-38mm (roughly 1 to 1.5 inches) - about the size of a large postage stamp when wings are spread

idTips.label: Resting posture
idTips.description: When at rest, holds wings in a distinctive tent-like position over the body with prominent tufts of fuzzy scales creating a bumpy, textured appearance

idTips.label: Body texture
idTips.description: Fuzzy, moth-like body that feels soft to the touch if handled, with dense scales that give it a somewhat chunky, robust appearance

idTips.label: Coloration
idTips.description: Generally muted earth tones with the pale sigmoid marking contrasting against darker wing background - colors help it blend with tree bark during daytime rest

habitat: Look for Sigmoid Prominents in areas with poplar and willow trees, since these are the only plants their caterpillars can eat. They're commonly found in wetland edges, stream corridors, and mixed forests where these trees grow naturally. Adults are attracted to outdoor lights near wooded areas, making porch lights and street lamps good places to spot them on warm nights.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in May and can be found at lights during warm evenings. This is when mated females are laying eggs on poplar and willow leaves.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight season continues through summer months with adults most active at night. Caterpillars are feeding on host trees during this time, though they're well-camouflaged and rarely seen.
seasonality.fall: Flight season typically ends by August, though some individuals may linger into early fall in warmer areas. Caterpillars complete development and pupate before winter.
seasonality.winter: Adults are not present - the species overwinters in the pupal stage, hidden in soil or leaf litter beneath their host trees until the following spring.

funFact: Sigmoid Prominent caterpillars have an amazing defense strategy - when threatened, they can shoot a stream of liquid from their mouth up to several inches away, essentially 'spitting' at potential predators to startle them and buy time to escape!
confusionNotes: Since this is the only Clostera species commonly found in New England, confusion with close relatives is unlikely. It might be confused with other prominent moths, but the distinctive sigmoid (S-shaped) wing marking is unique - remember 'S for Sigmoid' to separate it from other chunky, fuzzy moths in the family.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'prominent' in moth names doesn't refer to being well-known or important, but rather to the prominent tufts and bumps of scales that stick out from their wings and bodies, giving them their characteristic lumpy appearance when at rest.
compareHints: As the only Clostera species regularly found in New England, the Sigmoid Prominent stands alone in its genus here. Compared to other prominent moths in the Notodontidae family, it's distinguished by its characteristic S-shaped wing marking and medium size. While other prominent moths may have tufts and earth-tone coloring, none have that distinctive sigmoid curve that makes this species unmistakable.
